- Stephen Sugden
- is8ac

Thank you!

## Examples

You can directly embed JavaScript code into Rust:

```
let message = "Hello, 世界!";
let result = js! ;
println!;
```
Closures are also supported:

```
let print_hello = ;
js!
```
You can also pass arbitrary structures thanks to [serde](https://serde.rs/):

```
js_serializable!;
js! ;
```
This crate also exposes a number of Web APIs, for example:

```
let button = document.query_selector.unwrap.unwrap;
button.add_event_listener;
```
Exposing Rust functions to JavaScript is supported too:

```
```
Then you can do this from Node.js:

```
var hasher = require; // Where `hasher.js` is generated from Rust code.
console.log;
```
Or you can take the same `.js` file and use it in a web browser:

```

```
If you're using [Parcel](https://parceljs.org/) you can also use our [experimental Parcel plugin](https://github.com/koute/parcel-plugin-cargo-web);
first do this in your existing Parcel project:

```
$ npm install --save parcel-plugin-cargo-web
```
And then simply:

```
import hasher from "./hasher/Cargo.toml";
console.log;
```
## Design goals

- Expose a full suite of Web APIs as exposed by web browsers.
- Try to follow the original JavaScript conventions and structure as much as possible, except in cases where doing otherwise results in a clearly superior design.
- Be a building block from which higher level frameworks and libraries can be built.
- Make it convenient and easy to embed JavaScript code directly into Rust and to marshal data between the two.
- Integrate with the wider Rust ecosystem, e.g. support marshaling of structs which implement serde's Serializable.
- Put Rust in the driver's seat where a non-trivial Web application can be written without touching JavaScript at all.
- Allow Rust to take part in the upcoming WebAssembly (re)volution.
- Make it possible to trivially create standalone libraries which are easily callable from JavaScript.

## Getting started

Take a look at some of the examples:

- `examples/minimal`- a totally minimal example which calls- [alert](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/alert)
- `examples/todomvc`- a naively implemented- [TodoMVC](http://todomvc.com/)application; shows how to call into the DOM
- `examples/hasher`- shows how to export Rust functions to JavaScript and how to call them from a vanilla web browser environment or from Nodejs
- `examples/hasher-parcel`- shows how to import and call exported Rust functions in a- [Parcel](https://parceljs.org/)project
- `pinky-web`- [precompiled version here](http://koute.github.io/pinky-web/)

[The API documentation](https://docs.rs/stdweb/*/stdweb/) is also available for you to look at.

## Running the examples

-
Install [cargo-web](https://github.com/koute/cargo-web):`$ cargo install -f cargo-web`
-
Go into `examples/todomvc`and start the example using one of these commands:-
Compile to [WebAssembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly)using Rust's native WebAssembly backend:`$ cargo web start --target=wasm32-unknown-unknown`
-
Compile to [asm.js](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asm.js)using Emscripten:`$ cargo web start --target=asmjs-unknown-emscripten`
-
Compile to [WebAssembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly)using Emscripten:`$ cargo web start --target=wasm32-unknown-emscripten`

-
-
Visit `http://localhost:8000`with your browser.

For the `*-emscripten` targets `cargo-web` is not necessary, however
the native `wasm32-unknown-unknown` which doesn't need Emscripten
**requires** `cargo-web` to work!

# stdweb 0.4.17 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/stdweb/0.4.17

# A standard library for the client-side Web

The goal of this crate is to provide Rust bindings to the Web APIs and to allow a high degree of interoperability between Rust and JavaScript.

## Donate

## Patrons

This software was brought to you thanks to these wonderful people:

- Embark Studios
- Joe Narvaez
- Eduard Knyshov
- Anselm Eickhoff
- Johan Andersson
- Stephen Sugden
- is8ac

Thank you!

## Examples

You can directly embed JavaScript code into Rust:

```
let message = "Hello, 世界!";
let result = js! ;
println!;
```
Closures are also supported:

```
let print_hello = ;
js!
```
You can also pass arbitrary structures thanks to [serde](https://serde.rs/):

```
js_serializable!;
js! ;
```
This crate also exposes a number of Web APIs, for example:

```
let button = document.query_selector.unwrap.unwrap;
button.add_event_listener;
```
Exposing Rust functions to JavaScript is supported too:

```
```
Then you can do this from Node.js:

```
var hasher = require; // Where `hasher.js` is generated from Rust code.
console.log;
```
Or you can take the same `.js` file and use it in a web browser:

```

```
If you're using [Parcel](https://parceljs.org/) you can also use our [experimental Parcel plugin](https://github.com/koute/parcel-plugin-cargo-web);
first do this in your existing Parcel project:

```
$ npm install --save parcel-plugin-cargo-web
```
And then simply:

```
import hasher from "./hasher/Cargo.toml";
console.log;
```
## Design goals

- Expose a full suite of Web APIs as exposed by web browsers.
- Try to follow the original JavaScript conventions and structure as much as possible, except in cases where doing otherwise results in a clearly superior design.
- Be a building block from which higher level frameworks and libraries can be built.
- Make it convenient and easy to embed JavaScript code directly into Rust and to marshal data between the two.
- Integrate with the wider Rust ecosystem, e.g. support marshaling of structs which implement serde's Serializable.
- Put Rust in the driver's seat where a non-trivial Web application can be written without touching JavaScript at all.
- Allow Rust to take part in the upcoming WebAssembly (re)volution.
- Make it possible to trivially create standalone libraries which are easily callable from JavaScript.

## Getting started

Take a look at some of the examples:

- `examples/minimal`- a totally minimal example which calls- [alert](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/alert)
- `examples/todomvc`- a naively implemented- [TodoMVC](http://todomvc.com/)application; shows how to call into the DOM
- `examples/hasher`- shows how to export Rust functions to JavaScript and how to call them from a vanilla web browser environment or from Nodejs
- `examples/hasher-parcel`- shows how to import and call exported Rust functions in a- [Parcel](https://parceljs.org/)project
- `pinky-web`- [precompiled version here](http://koute.github.io/pinky-web/)

[The API documentation](https://docs.rs/stdweb/*/stdweb/) is also available for you to look at.

## Running the examples

-
Install [cargo-web](https://github.com/koute/cargo-web):`$ cargo install -f cargo-web`
-
Go into `examples/todomvc`and start the example using one of these commands:-
Compile to [WebAssembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly)using Rust's native WebAssembly backend:`$ cargo web start --target=wasm32-unknown-unknown`
-
Compile to [asm.js](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asm.js)using Emscripten:`$ cargo web start --target=asmjs-unknown-emscripten`
-
Compile to [WebAssembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly)using Emscripten:`$ cargo web start --target=wasm32-unknown-emscripten`

-
-
Visit `http://localhost:8000`with your browser.

For the `*-emscripten` targets `cargo-web` is not necessary, however
the native `wasm32-unknown-unknown` which doesn't need Emscripten
**requires** `cargo-web` to work!

## Design goals

- Expose a full suite of Web APIs as exposed by web browsers.
- Try to follow the original JavaScript conventions and structure as much as possible, except in cases where doing otherwise results in a clearly superior design.
- Be a building block from which higher level frameworks and libraries can be built.
- Make it convenient and easy to embed JavaScript code directly into Rust and to marshal data between the two.
- Integrate with the wider Rust ecosystem, e.g. support marshaling of structs which implement serde's Serializable.
- Put Rust in the driver's seat where a non-trivial Web application can be written without touching JavaScript at all.
- Allow Rust to take part in the upcoming WebAssembly (re)volution.
- Make it possible to trivially create standalone libraries which are easily callable from JavaScript.

## Getting started

Take a look at some of the examples:

- `examples/minimal`- a totally minimal example which calls- [alert](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/alert)
- `examples/todomvc`- a naively implemented- [TodoMVC](http://todomvc.com/)application; shows how to call into the DOM
- `examples/hasher`- shows how to export Rust functions to JavaScript and how to call them from a vanilla web browser environment or from Nodejs
- `examples/hasher-parcel`- shows how to import and call exported Rust functions in a- [Parcel](https://parceljs.org/)project
- `pinky-web`- [precompiled version here](http://koute.github.io/pinky-web/)

[The API documentation](https://docs.rs/stdweb/*/stdweb/) is also available for you to look at.

## Running the examples

-
Install [cargo-web](https://github.com/koute/cargo-web):`$ cargo install -f cargo-web`
-
Go into `examples/todomvc`and start the example using one of these commands:-
Compile to [WebAssembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly)using Rust's native WebAssembly backend:`$ cargo web start --target=wasm32-unknown-unknown`
-
Compile to [asm.js](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asm.js)using Emscripten:`$ cargo web start --target=asmjs-unknown-emscripten`
-
Compile to [WebAssembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly)using Emscripten:`$ cargo web start --target=wasm32-unknown-emscripten`

-
-
Visit `http://localhost:8000`with your browser.

For the `*-emscripten` targets `cargo-web` is not necessary, however
the native `wasm32-unknown-unknown` which doesn't need Emscripten
**requires** `cargo-web` to work!

# stdweb 0.4.15 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/stdweb/0.4.15

# A standard library for the client-side Web

The goal of this crate is to provide Rust bindings to the Web APIs and to allow a high degree of interoperability between Rust and JavaScript.

## Donate

## Patrons

## Examples

You can directly embed JavaScript code into Rust:

```
let message = "Hello, 世界!";
let result = js! ;
println!;
```
Closures are also supported:

```
let print_hello = ;
js!
```
You can also pass arbitrary structures thanks to [serde](https://serde.rs/):

```
js_serializable!;
js! ;
```
This crate also exposes a number of Web APIs, for example:

```
let button = document.query_selector.unwrap.unwrap;
button.add_event_listener;
```
Exposing Rust functions to JavaScript is supported too:

```
```
Then you can do this from Node.js:

```
var hasher = require; // Where `hasher.js` is generated from Rust code.
console.log;
```
Or you can take the same `.js` file and use it in a web browser:

```

```
If you're using [Parcel](https://parceljs.org/) you can also use our [experimental Parcel plugin](https://github.com/koute/parcel-plugin-cargo-web);
first do this in your existing Parcel project:

```
$ npm install --save parcel-plugin-cargo-web
```
And then simply:

```
import hasher from "./hasher/Cargo.toml";
console.log;
```
## Design goals

- Expose a full suite of Web APIs as exposed by web browsers.
- Try to follow the original JavaScript conventions and structure as much as possible, except in cases where doing otherwise results in a clearly superior design.
- Be a building block from which higher level frameworks and libraries can be built.
- Make it convenient and easy to embed JavaScript code directly into Rust and to marshal data between the two.
- Integrate with the wider Rust ecosystem, e.g. support marshaling of structs which implement serde's Serializable.
- Put Rust in the driver's seat where a non-trivial Web application can be written without touching JavaScript at all.
- Allow Rust to take part in the upcoming WebAssembly (re)volution.
- Make it possible to trivially create standalone libraries which are easily callable from JavaScript.

## Getting started

Take a look at some of the examples:

- `examples/minimal`- a totally minimal example which calls- [alert](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/alert)
- `examples/todomvc`- a naively implemented- [TodoMVC](http://todomvc.com/)application; shows how to call into the DOM
- `examples/hasher`- shows how to export Rust functions to JavaScript and how to call them from a vanilla web browser environment or from Nodejs
- `examples/hasher-parcel`- shows how to import and call exported Rust functions in a- [Parcel](https://parceljs.org/)project
- `pinky-web`- [precompiled version here](http://koute.github.io/pinky-web/)

[The API documentation](https://docs.rs/stdweb/*/stdweb/) is also available for you to look at.

## Running the examples

-
Install [cargo-web](https://github.com/koute/cargo-web):`$ cargo install -f cargo-web`
-
Go into `examples/todomvc`and start the example using one of these commands:-
Compile to [WebAssembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly)using Rust's native WebAssembly backend:`$ cargo web start --target=wasm32-unknown-unknown`
-
Compile to [asm.js](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asm.js)using Emscripten:`$ cargo web start --target=asmjs-unknown-emscripten`
-
Compile to [WebAssembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly)using Emscripten:`$ cargo web start --target=wasm32-unknown-emscripten`

-
-
Visit `http://localhost:8000`with your browser.

For the `*-emscripten` targets `cargo-web` is not necessary, however
the native `wasm32-unknown-unknown` which doesn't need Emscripten
**requires** `cargo-web` to work!

`wasm-bindgen` compatibility

This crate is currently **not** compatible with `wasm-bindgen`,
however adding such compatibility *is* planned in the near future.

# stdweb 0.4.14 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/stdweb/0.4.14

# A standard library for the client-side Web

The goal of this crate is to provide Rust bindings to the Web APIs and to allow a high degree of interoperability between Rust and JavaScript.

## Donate

## Patrons

This software was brought to you thanks to these wonderful people:

- Embark Studios
- Eduard Knyshov
- Anselm Eickhoff
- Johan Andersson
- Stephen Sugden
- is8ac

Thank you!

## Examples

You can directly embed JavaScript code into Rust:

```
let message = "Hello, 世界!";
let result = js! ;
println!;
```
Closures are also supported:

```
let print_hello = ;
js!
```
You can also pass arbitrary structures thanks to [serde](https://serde.rs/):

```
js_serializable!;
js! ;
```
This crate also exposes a number of Web APIs, for example:

```
let button = document.query_selector.unwrap.unwrap;
button.add_event_listener;
```
Exposing Rust functions to JavaScript is supported too:

```
```
Then you can do this from Node.js:

```
var hasher = require; // Where `hasher.js` is generated from Rust code.
console.log;
```
Or you can take the same `.js` file and use it in a web browser:

```

```
If you're using [Parcel](https://parceljs.org/) you can also use our [experimental Parcel plugin](https://github.com/koute/parcel-plugin-cargo-web);
first do this in your existing Parcel project:

```
$ npm install --save parcel-plugin-cargo-web
```
And then simply:

```
import hasher from "./hasher/Cargo.toml";
console.log;
```
## Design goals

- Expose a full suite of Web APIs as exposed by web browsers.
- Try to follow the original JavaScript conventions and structure as much as possible, except in cases where doing otherwise results in a clearly superior design.
- Be a building block from which higher level frameworks and libraries can be built.
- Make it convenient and easy to embed JavaScript code directly into Rust and to marshal data between the two.
- Integrate with the wider Rust ecosystem, e.g. support marshaling of structs which implement serde's Serializable.
- Put Rust in the driver's seat where a non-trivial Web application can be written without touching JavaScript at all.
- Allow Rust to take part in the upcoming WebAssembly (re)volution.
- Make it possible to trivially create standalone libraries which are easily callable from JavaScript.

## Getting started

Take a look at some of the examples:

- `examples/minimal`- a totally minimal example which calls- [alert](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/alert)
- `examples/todomvc`- a naively implemented- [TodoMVC](http://todomvc.com/)application; shows how to call into the DOM
- `examples/hasher`- shows how to export Rust functions to JavaScript and how to call them from a vanilla web browser environment or from Nodejs
- `examples/hasher-parcel`- shows how to import and call exported Rust functions in a- [Parcel](https://parceljs.org/)project
- `pinky-web`- [precompiled version here](http://koute.github.io/pinky-web/)

## Running the examples

-
Install [cargo-web](https://github.com/koute/cargo-web):`$ cargo install -f cargo-web`
-
Go into `examples/todomvc`and start the example using one of these commands:-
Compile to [WebAssembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly)using Rust's native WebAssembly backend:`$ cargo web start --target=wasm32-unknown-unknown`
-
Compile to [asm.js](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asm.js)using Emscripten:`$ cargo web start --target=asmjs-unknown-emscripten`
-
Compile to [WebAssembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly)using Emscripten:`$ cargo web start --target=wasm32-unknown-emscripten`

-
-
Visit `http://localhost:8000`with your browser.

For the `*-emscripten` targets `cargo-web` is not necessary, however
the native `wasm32-unknown-unknown` which doesn't need Emscripten
**requires** `cargo-web` to work!

`wasm-bindgen` compatibility

This crate is currently **not** compatible with `wasm-bindgen`,
however adding such compatibility *is* planned in the near future.

## Design goals

- Expose a full suite of Web APIs as exposed by web browsers.
- Try to follow the original JavaScript conventions and structure as much as possible, except in cases where doing otherwise results in a clearly superior design.
- Be a building block from which higher level frameworks and libraries can be built.
- Make it convenient and easy to embed JavaScript code directly into Rust and to marshal data between the two.
- Integrate with the wider Rust ecosystem, e.g. support marshaling of structs which implement serde's Serializable.
- Put Rust in the driver's seat where a non-trivial Web application can be written without touching JavaScript at all.
- Allow Rust to take part in the upcoming WebAssembly (re)volution.
- Make it possible to trivially create standalone libraries which are easily callable from JavaScript.

## Getting started

Take a look at some of the examples:

- `examples/minimal`- a totally minimal example which calls- [alert](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/alert)
- `examples/todomvc`- a naively implemented- [TodoMVC](http://todomvc.com/)application; shows how to call into the DOM
- `examples/hasher`- shows how to export Rust functions to JavaScript and how to call them from a vanilla web browser environment or from Nodejs
- `examples/hasher-parcel`- shows how to import and call exported Rust functions in a- [Parcel](https://parceljs.org/)project
- `pinky-web`- [precompiled version here](http://koute.github.io/pinky-web/)

## Running the examples

-
Install [cargo-web](https://github.com/koute/cargo-web):`$ cargo install -f cargo-web`
-
Go into `examples/todomvc`and start the example using one of these commands:-
Compile to [WebAssembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly)using Rust's native WebAssembly backend:`$ cargo web start --target=wasm32-unknown-unknown`
-
Compile to [asm.js](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asm.js)using Emscripten:`$ cargo web start --target=asmjs-unknown-emscripten`
-
Compile to [WebAssembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly)using Emscripten:`$ cargo web start --target=wasm32-unknown-emscripten`

-
-
Visit `http://localhost:8000`with your browser.

For the `*-emscripten` targets `cargo-web` is not necessary, however
the native `wasm32-unknown-unknown` which doesn't need Emscripten
**requires** `cargo-web` to work!

# stdweb 0.4.12 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/stdweb/0.4.12

# A standard library for the client-side Web

The goal of this crate is to provide Rust bindings to the Web APIs and to allow a high degree of interoperability between Rust and JavaScript.

## Examples

You can directly embed JavaScript code into Rust:

```
let message = "Hello, 世界!";
let result = js! ;
println!;
```
Closures are also supported:

```
let print_hello = ;
js!
```
You can also pass arbitrary structures thanks to [serde](https://serde.rs/):

```
js_serializable!;
js! ;
```
This crate also exposes a number of Web APIs, for example:

```
let button = document.query_selector.unwrap.unwrap;
button.add_event_listener;
```
Exposing Rust functions to JavaScript is supported too:

```
```
Then you can do this from Node.js:

```
var hasher = require; // Where `hasher.js` is generated from Rust code.
console.log;
```
Or you can take the same `.js` file and use it in a web browser:

```

```
If you're using [Parcel](https://parceljs.org/) you can also use our [experimental Parcel plugin](https://github.com/koute/parcel-plugin-cargo-web);
first do this in your existing Parcel project:

```
$ npm install --save parcel-plugin-cargo-web
```
And then simply:

```
import hasher from "./hasher/Cargo.toml";
console.log;
```
## Design goals

- Expose a full suite of Web APIs as exposed by web browsers.
- Try to follow the original JavaScript conventions and structure as much as possible, except in cases where doing otherwise results in a clearly superior design.
- Be a building block from which higher level frameworks and libraries can be built.
- Make it convenient and easy to embed JavaScript code directly into Rust and to marshal data between the two.
- Integrate with the wider Rust ecosystem, e.g. support marshaling of structs which implement serde's Serializable.
- Put Rust in the driver's seat where a non-trivial Web application can be written without touching JavaScript at all.
- Allow Rust to take part in the upcoming WebAssembly (re)volution.
- Make it possible to trivially create standalone libraries which are easily callable from JavaScript.

# stdweb 0.4.11 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/stdweb/0.4.11

# A standard library for the client-side Web

The goal of this crate is to provide Rust bindings to the Web APIs and to allow a high degree of interoperability between Rust and JavaScript.

## Donate

## Patrons

- Embark Studios

## Examples

You can directly embed JavaScript code into Rust:

```
let message = "Hello, 世界!";
let result = js! ;
println!;
```
Closures are also supported:

```
let print_hello = ;
js!
```
You can also pass arbitrary structures thanks to [serde](https://serde.rs/):

```
js_serializable!;
js! ;
```
This crate also exposes a number of Web APIs, for example:

```
let button = document.query_selector.unwrap.unwrap;
button.add_event_listener;
```
Exposing Rust functions to JavaScript is supported too:

```
```
Then you can do this from Node.js:

```
var hasher = require; // Where `hasher.js` is generated from Rust code.
console.log;
```
Or you can take the same `.js` file and use it in a web browser:

```

```
If you're using [Parcel](https://parceljs.org/) you can also use our [experimental Parcel plugin](https://github.com/koute/parcel-plugin-cargo-web);
first do this in your existing Parcel project:

```
$ npm install --save parcel-plugin-cargo-web
```
And then simply:

```
import hasher from "./hasher/Cargo.toml";
console.log;
```
## Design goals

- Expose a full suite of Web APIs as exposed by web browsers.
- Try to follow the original JavaScript conventions and structure as much as possible, except in cases where doing otherwise results in a clearly superior design.
- Be a building block from which higher level frameworks and libraries can be built.
- Make it convenient and easy to embed JavaScript code directly into Rust and to marshal data between the two.
- Integrate with the wider Rust ecosystem, e.g. support marshaling of structs which implement serde's Serializable.
- Put Rust in the driver's seat where a non-trivial Web application can be written without touching JavaScript at all.
- Allow Rust to take part in the upcoming WebAssembly (re)volution.
- Make it possible to trivially create standalone libraries which are easily callable from JavaScript.

## Getting started

Take a look at some of the examples:

- `examples/minimal`- a totally minimal example which calls- [alert](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/alert)
- `examples/todomvc`- a naively implemented- [TodoMVC](http://todomvc.com/)application; shows how to call into the DOM
- `examples/hasher`- shows how to export Rust functions to JavaScript and how to call them from a vanilla web browser environment or from Nodejs
- `examples/hasher-parcel`- shows how to import and call exported Rust functions in a- [Parcel](https://parceljs.org/)project
- `pinky-web`- [precompiled version here](http://koute.github.io/pinky-web/)

## Running the examples

-
Install [cargo-web](https://github.com/koute/cargo-web):`$ cargo install -f cargo-web`
-
Go into `examples/todomvc`and start the example using one of these commands:-
Compile to [WebAssembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly)using Rust's native WebAssembly backend:`$ cargo web start --target=wasm32-unknown-unknown`
-
Compile to [asm.js](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asm.js)using Emscripten:`$ cargo web start --target=asmjs-unknown-emscripten`
-
Compile to [WebAssembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly)using Emscripten:`$ cargo web start --target=wasm32-unknown-emscripten`

-
-
Visit `http://localhost:8000`with your browser.

For the `*-emscripten` targets `cargo-web` is not necessary, however
the native `wasm32-unknown-unknown` which doesn't need Emscripten
**requires** `cargo-web` to work!

# A standard library for the client-side Web

The goal of this crate is to provide Rust bindings to the Web APIs and to allow a high degree of interoperability between Rust and JavaScript.

## Examples

You can directly embed JavaScript code into Rust:

```
let message = "Hello, 世界!";
let result = js! ;
println!;
```
Closures are also supported:

```
let print_hello = ;
js!
```
You can also pass arbitrary structures thanks to [serde](https://serde.rs/):

```
js_serializable!;
js! ;
```
This crate also exposes a number of Web APIs, for example:

```
let button = document.query_selector.unwrap.unwrap;
button.add_event_listener;
```
Exposing Rust functions to JavaScript is supported too:

```
```
Then you can do this from Node.js:

```
var hasher = require; // Where `hasher.js` is generated from Rust code.
console.log;
```
Or you can take the same `.js` file and use it in a web browser:

```

```
If you're using [Parcel](https://parceljs.org/) you can also use our [experimental Parcel plugin](https://github.com/koute/parcel-plugin-cargo-web);
first do this in your existing Parcel project:

```
$ npm install --save parcel-plugin-cargo-web
```
And then simply:

```
import hasher from "./hasher/Cargo.toml";
console.log;
```
## Design goals

- Expose a full suite of Web APIs as exposed by web browsers.
- Try to follow the original JavaScript conventions and structure as much as possible, except in cases where doing otherwise results in a clearly superior design.
- Be a building block from which higher level frameworks and libraries can be built.
- Make it convenient and easy to embed JavaScript code directly into Rust and to marshal data between the two.
- Integrate with the wider Rust ecosystem, e.g. support marshaling of structs which implement serde's Serializable.
- Put Rust in the driver's seat where a non-trivial Web application can be written without touching JavaScript at all.
- Allow Rust to take part in the upcoming WebAssembly (re)volution.
- Make it possible to trivially create standalone libraries which are easily callable from JavaScript.

## Getting started

Take a look at some of the examples:

- `examples/minimal`- a totally minimal example which calls- [alert](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/alert)
- `examples/todomvc`- a naively implemented- [TodoMVC](http://todomvc.com/)application; shows how to call into the DOM
- `examples/hasher`- shows how to export Rust functions to JavaScript and how to call them from a vanilla web browser environment or from Nodejs
- `examples/hasher-parcel`- shows how to import and call exported Rust functions in a- [Parcel](https://parceljs.org/)project
- `pinky-web`- [precompiled version here](http://koute.github.io/pinky-web/)

## Running the examples

-
Install [cargo-web](https://github.com/koute/cargo-web):`$ cargo install -f cargo-web`
-
Go into `examples/todomvc`and start the example using one of these commands:-
Compile to [WebAssembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly)using Rust's native WebAssembly backend (requires Rust nightly!):`$ cargo web start --target=wasm32-unknown-unknown`
-
Compile to [asm.js](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asm.js)using Emscripten:`$ cargo web start --target=asmjs-unknown-emscripten`
-
Compile to [WebAssembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly)using Emscripten:`$ cargo web start --target=wasm32-unknown-emscripten`

-
-
Visit `http://localhost:8000`with your browser.

For the `*-emscripten` targets `cargo-web` is not necessary, however
the native `wasm32-unknown-unknown` which doesn't need Emscripten
**requires** `cargo-web` to work!

# A standard library for the client-side Web

The goal of this crate is to provide Rust bindings to the Web APIs and to allow a high degree of interoperability between Rust and JavaScript.

## Donate

## Patrons

This software was brought to you thanks to these wonderful people:

- Eduard Knyshov
- Anselm Eickhoff
- Ferran Pujol Camins
- Johan Andersson
- Stephen Sugden

Thank you!

## Examples

You can directly embed JavaScript code into Rust:

```
let message = "Hello, 世界!";
let result = js! ;
println!;
```
Closures are also supported:

```
let print_hello = ;
js!
```
You can also pass arbitrary structures thanks to [serde](https://serde.rs/):

```
js_serializable!;
js! ;
```
This crate also exposes a number of Web APIs, for example:

```
let button = document.query_selector.unwrap.unwrap;
button.add_event_listener;
```
Exposing Rust functions to JavaScript is supported too:

```
```
Then you can do this from Node.js:

```
var hasher = require; // Where `hasher.js` is generated from Rust code.
console.log;
```
Or you can take the same `.js` file and use it in a web browser:

```

```
If you're using [Parcel](https://parceljs.org/) you can also use our [experimental Parcel plugin](https://github.com/koute/parcel-plugin-cargo-web);
first do this in your existing Parcel project:

```
$ npm install --save parcel-plugin-cargo-web
```
And then simply:

```
import hasher from "./hasher/Cargo.toml";
console.log;
```
## Design goals

- Expose a full suite of Web APIs as exposed by web browsers.
- Try to follow the original JavaScript conventions and structure as much as possible, except in cases where doing otherwise results in a clearly superior design.
- Be a building block from which higher level frameworks and libraries can be built.
- Make it convenient and easy to embed JavaScript code directly into Rust and to marshal data between the two.
- Integrate with the wider Rust ecosystem, e.g. support marshaling of structs which implement serde's Serializable.
- Put Rust in the driver's seat where a non-trivial Web application can be written without touching JavaScript at all.
- Allow Rust to take part in the upcoming WebAssembly (re)volution.
- Make it possible to trivially create standalone libraries which are easily callable from JavaScript.

## Getting started

Take a look at some of the examples:

- `examples/minimal`- a totally minimal example which calls- [alert](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/alert)
- `examples/todomvc`- a naively implemented- [TodoMVC](http://todomvc.com/)application; shows how to call into the DOM
- `examples/hasher`- shows how to export Rust functions to JavaScript and how to call them from a vanilla web browser environment or from Nodejs
- `examples/hasher-parcel`- shows how to import and call exported Rust functions in a- [Parcel](https://parceljs.org/)project
- `pinky-web`- [precompiled version here](http://koute.github.io/pinky-web/)

## Running the examples

-
Install [cargo-web](https://github.com/koute/cargo-web):`$ cargo install -f cargo-web`
-
Go into `examples/todomvc`and start the example using one of these commands:-
Compile to [WebAssembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly)using Rust's native WebAssembly backend (requires Rust nightly!):`$ cargo web start --target=wasm32-unknown-unknown`
-
Compile to [asm.js](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asm.js)using Emscripten:`$ cargo web start --target=asmjs-unknown-emscripten`
-
Compile to [WebAssembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly)using Emscripten:`$ cargo web start --target=wasm32-unknown-emscripten`

-
-
Visit `http://localhost:8000`with your browser.

For the `*-emscripten` targets `cargo-web` is not necessary, however
the native `wasm32-unknown-unknown` which doesn't need Emscripten
**requires** `cargo-web` to work!

## Design goals

- Expose a full suite of Web APIs as exposed by web browsers.
- Try to follow the original JavaScript conventions and structure as much as possible, except in cases where doing otherwise results in a clearly superior design.
- Be a building block from which higher level frameworks and libraries can be built.
- Make it convenient and easy to embed JavaScript code directly into Rust and to marshal data between the two.
- Integrate with the wider Rust ecosystem, e.g. support marshaling of structs which implement serde's Serializable.
- Put Rust in the driver's seat where a non-trivial Web application can be written without touching JavaScript at all.
- Allow Rust to take part in the upcoming WebAssembly (re)volution.
- Make it possible to trivially create standalone libraries which are easily callable from JavaScript.

## Getting started

Take a look at some of the examples:

- `examples/minimal`- a totally minimal example which calls- [alert](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/alert)
- `examples/todomvc`- a naively implemented- [TodoMVC](http://todomvc.com/)application; shows how to call into the DOM
- `examples/hasher`- shows how to export Rust functions to JavaScript and how to call them from a vanilla web browser environment or from Nodejs
- `examples/hasher-parcel`- shows how to import and call exported Rust functions in a- [Parcel](https://parceljs.org/)project
- `pinky-web`- [precompiled version here](http://koute.github.io/pinky-web/)

## Running the examples

-
Install [cargo-web](https://github.com/koute/cargo-web):`$ cargo install -f cargo-web`
-
Go into `examples/todomvc`and start the example using one of these commands:-
Compile to [WebAssembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly)using Rust's native WebAssembly backend (requires Rust nightly!):`$ cargo web start --target=wasm32-unknown-unknown`
-
Compile to [asm.js](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asm.js)using Emscripten:`$ cargo web start --target=asmjs-unknown-emscripten`
-
Compile to [WebAssembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly)using Emscripten:`$ cargo web start --target=wasm32-unknown-emscripten`

-
-
Visit `http://localhost:8000`with your browser.

For the `*-emscripten` targets `cargo-web` is not necessary, however
the native `wasm32-unknown-unknown` which doesn't need Emscripten
**requires** `cargo-web` to work!

- Integrate with the wider Rust ecosystem, e.g. support marshaling of structs which implement serde's Serializable.
- Put Rust in the driver's seat where a non-trivial Web application can be written without touching JavaScript at all.
- Allow Rust to take part in the upcoming WebAssembly (re)volution.
- Make it possible to trivially create standalone libraries which are easily callable from JavaScript.

## Getting started

Take a look at some of the examples:

- `examples/minimal`- a totally minimal example which calls- [alert](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/alert)
- `examples/todomvc`- a naively implemented- [TodoMVC](http://todomvc.com/)application; shows how to call into the DOM
- `examples/hasher`- shows how to export Rust functions to JavaScript and how to call them from a vanilla web browser environment or from Nodejs
- `examples/hasher-parcel`- shows how to import and call exported Rust functions in a- [Parcel](https://parceljs.org/)project
- `pinky-web`- [precompiled version here](http://koute.github.io/pinky-web/)

## Running the examples

-
Install [cargo-web](https://github.com/koute/cargo-web):`$ cargo install -f cargo-web`
-
Go into `examples/todomvc`and start the example using one of these commands:-
Compile to [WebAssembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly)using Rust's native WebAssembly backend (requires Rust nightly!):`$ cargo web start --target=wasm32-unknown-unknown`
-
Compile to [asm.js](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asm.js)using Emscripten:`$ cargo web start --target=asmjs-unknown-emscripten`
-
Compile to [WebAssembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly)using Emscripten:`$ cargo web start --target=wasm32-unknown-emscripten`

-
-
Visit `http://localhost:8000`with your browser.

For the `*-emscripten` targets `cargo-web` is not necessary, however
the native `wasm32-unknown-unknown` which doesn't need Emscripten
**requires** `cargo-web` to work!

# A standard library for the client-side Web

The goal of this crate is to provide Rust bindings to the Web APIs and to allow a high degree of interoperability between Rust and JavaScript.

## Donate

## Patrons

This software was brought to you thanks to these wonderful people:

- Daniel Norman
- Ben Berman
- Stephen Sugden

Thank you!

## Examples

You can directly embed JavaScript code into Rust:

```
let message = "Hello, 世界!";
let result = js! ;
println!;
```
Closures are also supported:

```
let print_hello = ;
js!
```
You can also pass arbitrary structures thanks to [serde](https://serde.rs/):

```
js_serializable!;
js! ;
```
This crate also exposes a number of Web APIs, for example:

```
let button = document.query_selector.unwrap.unwrap;
button.add_event_listener;
```
Exposing Rust functions to JavaScript is supported too:

```
```
Then you can do this from Node.js:

```
var hasher = require; // Where `hasher.js` is generated from Rust code.
console.log;
```
Or you can take the same `.js` file and use it in a web browser:

```

```
If you're using [Parcel](https://parceljs.org/) you can also use our [experimental Parcel plugin](https://github.com/koute/parcel-plugin-cargo-web);
first do this in your existing Parcel project:

```
$ npm install --save parcel-plugin-cargo-web
```
And then simply:

```
import hasher from "./hasher/Cargo.toml";
console.log;
```
## Design goals

- Expose a full suite of Web APIs as exposed by web browsers.
- Try to follow the original JavaScript conventions and structure as much as possible, except in cases where doing otherwise results in a clearly superior design.
- Be a building block from which higher level frameworks and libraries can be built.
- Make it convenient and easy to embed JavaScript code directly into Rust and to marshal data between the two.
- Integrate with the wider Rust ecosystem, e.g. support marshaling of structs which implement serde's Serializable.
- Put Rust in the driver's seat where a non-trivial Web application can be written without touching JavaScript at all.
- Allow Rust to take part in the upcoming WebAssembly (re)volution.
- Make it possible to trivially create standalone libraries which are easily callable from JavaScript.

Take a look at some of the examples:

- `examples/minimal`- a totally minimal example which calls- [alert](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/alert)

# A standard library for the client-side Web

The goal of this crate is to provide Rust bindings to the Web APIs and to allow a high degree of interoperability between Rust and JavaScript.

## Donate

## Patrons

This software was brought to you thanks to these wonderful people:

- Daniel Norman
- Ben Berman
- Stephen Sugden

Thank you!

## Examples

You can directly embed JavaScript code into Rust:

```
let message = "Hello, 世界!";
let result = js! ;
println!;
```
Closures are also supported:

```
let print_hello = ;
js!
```
You can also pass arbitrary structures thanks to [serde](https://serde.rs/):

```
js_serializable!;
js! ;
```
This crate also exposes a number of Web APIs, for example:

```
let button = document.query_selector.unwrap.unwrap;
button.add_event_listener;
```
Exposing Rust functions to JavaScript is supported too:

```
```
Then you can do this from Node.js:

```
var hasher = require; // Where `hasher.js` is generated from Rust code.
console.log;
```
Or you can take the same `.js` file and use it in a web browser:

```

```
If you're using [Parcel](https://parceljs.org/) you can also use our [experimental Parcel plugin](https://github.com/koute/parcel-plugin-cargo-web);
first do this in your existing Parcel project:

```
$ npm install --save parcel-plugin-cargo-web
```
And then simply:

```
import hasher from "./hasher/Cargo.toml";
console.log;
```
## Design goals

- Expose a full suite of Web APIs as exposed by web browsers.
- Try to follow the original JavaScript conventions and structure as much as possible, except in cases where doing otherwise results in a clearly superior design.
- Be a building block from which higher level frameworks and libraries can be built.
- Make it convenient and easy to embed JavaScript code directly into Rust and to marshal data between the two.
- Integrate with the wider Rust ecosystem, e.g. support marshaling of structs which implement serde's Serializable.
- Put Rust in the driver's seat where a non-trivial Web application can be written without touching JavaScript at all.
- Allow Rust to take part in the upcoming WebAssembly (re)volution.
- Make it possible to trivially create standalone libraries which are easily callable from JavaScript.

## Getting started

Take a look at some of the examples:

- `examples/minimal`- a totally minimal example which calls- [alert](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/alert)
- `examples/todomvc`- a naively implemented- [TodoMVC](http://todomvc.com/)application; shows how to call into the DOM
- `examples/hasher`- shows how to export Rust functions to JavaScript and how to call them from a vanilla web browser environment or from Nodejs
- `examples/hasher-parcel`- shows how to import and call exported Rust functions in a- [Parcel](https://parceljs.org/)project
- `pinky-web`- [precompiled version here](http://koute.github.io/pinky-web/)

## Running the examples

-
Install [cargo-web](https://github.com/koute/cargo-web):`$ cargo install -f cargo-web`
-
Go into `examples/todomvc`and start the example using one of these commands:-
Compile to [WebAssembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly)using Rust's native WebAssembly backend (requires Rust nightly!):`$ cargo web start --target=wasm32-unknown-unknown`
-
Compile to [asm.js](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asm.js)using Emscripten:`$ cargo web start --target=asmjs-unknown-emscripten`
-
Compile to [WebAssembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly)using Emscripten:`$ cargo web start --target=wasm32-unknown-emscripten`

-
-
Visit `http://localhost:8000`with your browser.

For the `*-emscripten` targets `cargo-web` is not necessary, however
the native `wasm32-unknown-unknown` which doesn't need Emscripten
**requires** `cargo-web` to work!

# stdweb 0.4.1 - Docs.rs

# A standard library for the client-side Web

The goal of this crate is to provide Rust bindings to the Web APIs and to allow a high degree of interoperability between Rust and JavaScript.

## Donate

## Patrons

This software was brought to you thanks to these wonderful people:

- Ben Berman

Thank you!

## Examples

You can directly embed JavaScript code into Rust:

```
let message = "Hello, 世界!";
let result = js! ;
println!;
```
Closures are also supported:

```
let print_hello = ;
js!
```
You can also pass arbitrary structures thanks to [serde](https://serde.rs/):

```
js_serializable!;
js! ;
```
This crate also exposes a number of Web APIs, for example:

```
let button = document.query_selector.unwrap.unwrap;
button.add_event_listener;
```
Exposing Rust functions to JavaScript is supported too:

```
```
Then you can do this from Node.js:

```
var hasher = require; // Where `hasher.js` is generated from Rust code.
console.log;
```
Or you can take the same `.js` file and use it in a web browser:

```

```
If you're using [Parcel](https://parceljs.org/) you can also use our [experimental Parcel plugin](https://github.com/koute/parcel-plugin-cargo-web);
first do this in your existing Parcel project:

```
$ npm install --save parcel-plugin-cargo-web
```
And then simply:

```
import hasher from "./hasher/Cargo.toml";
console.log;
```
## Design goals

- Expose a full suite of Web APIs as exposed by web browsers.
- Try to follow the original JavaScript conventions and structure as much as possible, except in cases where doing otherwise results in a clearly superior design.
- Be a building block from which higher level frameworks and libraries can be built.
- Make it convenient and easy to embed JavaScript code directly into Rust and to marshal data between the two.
- Integrate with the wider Rust ecosystem, e.g. support marshaling of structs which implement serde's Serializable.
- Put Rust in the driver's seat where a non-trivial Web application can be written without touching JavaScript at all.
- Allow Rust to take part in the upcoming WebAssembly (re)volution.
- Make it possible to trivially create standalone libraries which are easily callable from JavaScript.

## Getting started

Take a look at some of the examples:

- `examples/minimal`- a totally minimal example which calls- [alert](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/alert)
- `examples/todomvc`- a naively implemented- [TodoMVC](http://todomvc.com/)application; shows how to call into the DOM
- `examples/hasher`- shows how to export Rust functions to JavaScript and how to call them from a vanilla web browser environment or from Nodejs
- `examples/hasher-parcel`- shows how to import and call exported Rust functions in a- [Parcel](https://parceljs.org/)project
- `pinky-web`- [precompiled version here](http://koute.github.io/pinky-web/)

## Running the examples

-
Install [cargo-web](https://github.com/koute/cargo-web):`$ cargo install -f cargo-web`
-
Go into `examples/todomvc`and start the example using one of these commands:-
Compile to [WebAssembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly)using Rust's native WebAssembly backend (requires Rust nightly!):`$ cargo web start --target=wasm32-unknown-unknown`
-
Compile to [asm.js](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asm.js)using Emscripten:`$ cargo web start --target=asmjs-unknown-emscripten`
-
Compile to [WebAssembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly)using Emscripten:`$ cargo web start --target=wasm32-unknown-emscripten`

-
-
Visit `http://localhost:8000`with your browser.

For the `*-emscripten` targets `cargo-web` is not necessary, however
the native `wasm32-unknown-unknown` which doesn't need Emscripten
**requires** `cargo-web` to work!

## Running the examples

-
Add one of Rust's Web targets with rustup. -
For compiling to asmjs through Emscripten: `$ rustup target add asmjs-unknown-emscripten`
-
For compiling to WebAssembly through Emscripten: `$ rustup target add wasm32-unknown-emscripten`
-
For compiling to WebAssembly through Rust's native backend: `$ rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown`

-
-
Install [cargo-web](https://github.com/koute/cargo-web):`$ cargo install -f cargo-web`
-
Go into `examples/todomvc`and start the example.-
For the `asmjs-unknown-emscripten`backend:`$ cargo web start --target-asmjm-emscripten`
-
For the `wasm32-unknown-emscripten`:`$ cargo web start --target-webasm-emscripten`
-
For the `wasm32-unknown-unknown`:`$ cargo web start --target-webasm`

-
-
Visit `http://localhost:8000`with your browser.

For the `*-emscripten` targets `cargo-web` is not neccessary, however
the native `wasm32-unknown-unknown` which doesn't need Emscripten
**requires** `cargo-web` to work!

## Exposing Rust functions to JavaScript

* WARNING*: This is only supported for Rust's native

`wasm32-unknown-unknown` target!(Note: this is based on the `examples/hasher` example)

With the `stdweb` crate you can easily expose a Rust function
to JavaScript like this:

```
extern crate stdweb;
extern crate sha1;
use Sha1;
```
If you compile this code with `cargo-web build --target-webasm` you'll get two files:

- `target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/hasher.js`
- `target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/hasher.wasm`

You can copy them into your JavaScript project and load like any other JavaScript file:

```
```
After it's loaded you can access `Rust.hasher`, which is a [Promise](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise) which
will resolve once the WebAssembly module is loaded. Inside that promise
you'll find the contents of `Module.exports` which we've set from our
Rust code, which includes our exported function which you can now call:

```

```
You can also use the very same `hasher.js` from Nodejs:

```
const hasher = require;
const string = "fiddlesticks";
const hash = hasher.;
console.log;
```
For the Nodejs environment the WebAssembly is compiled synchronously.

- Make it possible to trivially create standalone libraries which are easily callable from JavaScript.

Take a look at some of the examples:

- `examples/minimal`- a totally minimal example which calls- [alert](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/alert)
- `examples/todomvc`- a naively implemented- [TodoMVC](http://todomvc.com/)application; shows how to call into the DOM
- `examples/hasher`- shows how to export Rust functions to JavaScript and how to call them from the browser or Nodejs

## Running the examples

-

-

## Exposing Rust functions to JavaScript

* WARNING*: This is only supported for Rust's native

`wasm32-unknown-unknown` target!(Note: this is based on the `examples/hasher` example)

- `target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/hasher.wasm`

```
```

will resolve once the WebAssembly module is loaded. Inside that promise
you'll find the contents of `Module.exports` which we've set from our
Rust code, which includes our exported function which you can now call:

```

```
You can also use the very same `hasher.js` from Nodejs:

console.log;
```
For the Nodejs environment the WebAssembly is compiled synchronously.

# discard - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/discard/1.0.4/target-redirect/discard/

## Expand description

There are situations where you need to intentionally leak *some*
memory but not *other* memory. This crate can help!

But before I explain, you are probably wondering: why would I want to leak memory in the first place?

There are certain rare situations where leaking memory is either
desirable or *necessary*.

As an example, let’s say I am using [stdweb](https://crates.io/crates/stdweb),
which lets me use JavaScript APIs in Rust.

So I write some code like this:

Seems reasonable, right? But there’s a problem: the `add_event_listener` method
returns an `EventListenerHandle`, and when the `EventListenerHandle` is dropped it
will remove the event listener.

Because I’m not using the `EventListenerHandle`, it is immediately dropped, so it
receives no events!

Okay, no problem, just use [ std::mem::forget](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/mem/fn.forget.html):

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// This will automatically remove the event listener when `handle` is dropped
let handle = node.add_event_listener(|event: ClickEvent| {
    // ...
});
// Now it will no longer remove the event listener
std::mem::forget(handle);
```
Now the event listener will remain alive forever, which is what I want.

But there’s two problems with this:

-
I want it to keep the event listener alive forever, but I *also*want it to clean up any unused internal memory. Using`std::mem::forget`**all**
-
There are situations where I want to leak the event listener, and then later *unleak*it. That’s not possible with`std::mem::forget`

The solution to all of these problems is:

-
The `EventListenerHandle`should**not**`Drop`
-
The `EventListenerHandle`should implement the`Discard`
-
The `add_event_listener`method should return`DiscardOnDrop<EventListenerHandle>`.

Now let’s look at what is possible:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// This will automatically remove the event listener when `handle` is dropped
let handle = node.add_event_listener(|event: ClickEvent| {
    // ...
});
// Now it will no longer remove the event listener, this is similar to `std::mem::forget`
let leaked = DiscardOnDrop::leak(handle);
// Now it will remove the event listener, even though it was leaked
leaked.discard();
```
There’s two huge differences between [ DiscardOnDrop::leak](https://docs.rs/struct.DiscardOnDrop.html#method.leak)
and

[:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/mem/fn.forget.html)

`std::mem::forget`-
`std::mem::forget`**all**`DiscardOnDrop::leak`*minimal*amount of memory: unused memory is properly cleaned up.
-
With `std::mem::forget``DiscardOnDrop::leak`

Most of the time you don’t need to worry about any of this:
[ DiscardOnDrop](https://docs.rs/struct.DiscardOnDrop.html) will automatically call

[when it is dropped, so in that situation](https://docs.rs/trait.Discard.html#tymethod.discard)

`discard`[behaves the same as](https://docs.rs/trait.Discard.html)

`Discard`[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ops/trait.Drop.html)

`Drop`So you can use normal Rust idioms, and everything works as you would expect. You only need to
worry about [ Discard](https://docs.rs/trait.Discard.html) when you need to intentionally leak some memory.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Discard](https://docs.rs/struct.DiscardOnDrop.html)- OnDrop
- If you have a value which implements `Discard``DiscardOnDrop::new(value)``value.discard()`

# Discard in discard - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/discard/^1.0.3/trait.Discard.html

```
pub trait Discard {
    // Required method
    fn
```
[discard](https://docs.rs#tymethod.discard)(self);
}## Expand description

This trait is very similar to [ Drop](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ops/trait.Drop.html):
it allows for cleaning up memory and resources when they are no longer needed.

However, unlike [ Drop](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ops/trait.Drop.html) you need to
manually call the

[method.](https://docs.rs#tymethod.discard)

`discard`It is extremely common to use [ DiscardOnDrop](https://docs.rs/struct.DiscardOnDrop.html), which will cause it
to automatically call the

[method when it is dropped. In that situation](https://docs.rs#tymethod.discard)

`discard`[behaves exactly the same as](https://docs.rs/trait.Discard.html)

`Discard`[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ops/trait.Drop.html)

`Drop`You can use [ DiscardOnDrop::leak](https://docs.rs/struct.DiscardOnDrop.html#method.leak) to intentionally leak the value
(which causes

[to not be called), and then later you can manually call](https://docs.rs#tymethod.discard)

`discard`[to clean up the resources, even after the resources have been leaked.](https://docs.rs#tymethod.discard)

`discard`See the [module documentation](https://docs.rs/index.html) for more details.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# DiscardOnDrop in discard - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/discard/^1.0.3/struct.DiscardOnDrop.html

`pub struct DiscardOnDrop<A: `[Discard](https://docs.rs/trait.Discard.html)>(/* private fields */);## Expand description

If you have a value which implements [ Discard](https://docs.rs/trait.Discard.html), you can use

[which will wrap the value. When the wrapper is dropped it will automatically call](https://docs.rs/struct.DiscardOnDrop.html#method.new)

`DiscardOnDrop::new(value)`[.](https://docs.rs/trait.Discard.html#tymethod.discard)

`value.discard()`You can use the [ DiscardOnDrop::leak](https://docs.rs#method.leak) function to unwrap it (which returns

`value`). This causes
it to no longer call [when it is dropped, which means it will leak memory unless you manually call](https://docs.rs/trait.Discard.html#tymethod.discard)

`discard`[.](https://docs.rs/trait.Discard.html#tymethod.discard)

`discard`See the [module documentation](https://docs.rs/index.html) for more details.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/discard/lib.rs.html#150-185)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-DiscardOnDrop%3CA%3E)### impl<A: [Discard](https://docs.rs/trait.Discard.html)> [DiscardOnDrop](https://docs.rs/struct.DiscardOnDrop.html)<A>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/discard/lib.rs.html#150-185)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-DiscardOnDrop%3CA%3E)

### impl<A: [Discard](https://docs.rs/trait.Discard.html)> [DiscardOnDrop](https://docs.rs/struct.DiscardOnDrop.html)<A>

Returns the wrapped `discarder`.

It will no longer automatically call [ discarder.discard()](https://docs.rs/trait.Discard.html#tymethod.discard), so this

*leak memory unless you manually call*

**will**[.](https://docs.rs/trait.Discard.html#tymethod.discard)

`discarder.discard()`See the [module documentation](https://docs.rs/index.html) for more details.

This is implemented as a function (*not* a method) so that way it doesn’t interfere with any of the
methods on `discarder`.

# futures_channel - Rust

Asynchronous channels.

This crate provides channels that can be used to communicate between asynchronous tasks.

All items of this library are only available when the `std` or `alloc` feature of this

| [mpsc](https://docs.rs/mpsc/index.html) | A multi-producer, single-consumer queue for sending values across asynchronous tasks. |
| [oneshot](https://docs.rs/oneshot/index.html) | A channel for sending a single message between asynchronous tasks. |

# futures_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/futures-core-preview/latest/target-redirect/futures_core/

## Expand description

Core traits and types for asynchronous operations in Rust.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use future::`- [Future](https://docs.rs/future/trait.Future.html);
- `pub use future::`- [IntoFuture](https://docs.rs/future/trait.IntoFuture.html);
- `pub use stream::`- [Stream](https://docs.rs/stream/trait.Stream.html);
- `pub use never::`- [Never](https://docs.rs/never/enum.Never.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [executor](https://docs.rs/executor/index.html)
- Executors.
- [future](https://docs.rs/future/index.html)
- Futures.
- [never](https://docs.rs/never/index.html)
- Definition and trait implementations for the `Never`type, a stand-in for the`!`type until it becomes stable.
- [stream](https://docs.rs/stream/index.html)
- Asynchronous streams.
- [task](https://docs.rs/task/index.html)
- Task notification.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [task_](https://docs.rs/macro.task_local.html)- local
- A macro to create a `static`of type`LocalKey`
- [try_](https://docs.rs/macro.try_ready.html)- ready
- A macro for extracting the successful type of a `Poll<T, E>`.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Async](https://docs.rs/enum.Async.html)
- Indicates whether a value is available, or if the current task has been scheduled for later wake-up instead.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Poll](https://docs.rs/type.Poll.html)
- A convenience wrapper for `Result<Async<T>, E>`.
